Application security groups for the web and database tiers
Augmented rules listing each server's IP address
Azure Virtual Network Manager network groups
questions.explain: ASGs let rules reference NIC groups, so scaling only changes group membership. Service tags represent Azure service prefixes, not your VMs. IP lists need updating as servers change. AVNM network groups contain whole virtual networks, not individual VMs.

questions.stem: For each statement about application security groups, select Yes if true.

statements.s: An ASG can contain network interfaces from two different virtual networks.
An NSG rule that references an ASG affects only NICs that are members of that ASG.
An ASG can be used as both the source and the destination of a single NSG rule.

questions.explain: All NICs in an ASG must be in the same VNet as the first member. Rules referencing an ASG apply only to its members, even when the NSG is on the subnet. One rule can use an ASG for source and another for destination, as long as both sets of NICs share a VNet.

questions.stem: Complete the Azure CLI command so the rule allows traffic only from members of AsgWeb to members of AsgDb.
questions.code:
az network nsg rule create \
  --resource-group rg-app --nsg-name nsg-db \
  --name AllowWebToDb --priority 100 \
  --access Allow --protocol Tcp --direction Inbound \
  ____ \
  --destination-asgs AsgDb --destination-port-ranges 1433
options: --source-asgs AsgWeb
--source-address-prefixes AsgWeb
--source-service-tag AsgWeb
--source-application-group AsgWeb
questions.explain: --source-asgs takes ASG names or IDs as the rule source. --source-address-prefixes expects IPs, CIDRs or service tags, not ASGs. The other two parameter names don't exist in az network nsg rule create.

questions.stem: A central network team needs a rule that guarantees vulnerability scanners can reach every production VNet on all ports, even if application teams add NSG rules that deny the traffic. Which Azure Virtual Network Manager security admin action should you use?
options: Allow
Deny
Always Allow
Allow with a priority of 1
questions.explain: Always Allow permits traffic and stops evaluation, so NSG rules can't block it. Allow, at any priority, still passes traffic on to NSG evaluation, where a Deny could block it. Deny is the opposite of what is needed.

questions.stem: New VNets tagged env=prod must automatically receive your Azure Virtual Network Manager security admin rules. How should you configure the network group?
options: Static membership, adding each VNet manually
An Azure Firewall policy with a parent and child hierarchy
An application security group per subscription
Dynamic membership using an Azure Policy condition on the tag
questions.explain: Dynamic membership uses Azure Policy conditions, such as a tag, so matching VNets join the network group automatically. Static membership needs manual changes. Firewall policies and ASGs aren't ways to define AVNM network group membership.

questions.stem: You need to block inbound SSH from the internet to all VNets in two subscriptions by using Azure Virtual Network Manager. Put the steps in order.
options: Create a Virtual Network Manager instance scoped to both subscriptions
Create a network group and add the virtual networks
Create a security admin configuration with a rule collection containing a Deny rule for TCP 22
Deploy the security admin configuration to the target regions
questions.explain: The AVNM instance's scope defines which VNets can be managed. Network groups pick the targets, the security admin configuration holds the rule collection aimed at the group, and nothing takes effect until the configuration is deployed to regions.

questions.stem: Which two statements about Azure Virtual Network Manager security admin rules are true? Select TWO.
options: Lower priority numbers have lower precedence
They are evaluated before NSG rules
They can only be applied to VNets in a single subscription
They replace NSGs, so NSGs on the subnets are removed
They apply only after a configuration is deployed
questions.explain: Security admin rules are evaluated before NSGs and take effect only after deployment. NSGs remain in place. AVNM scope can span management groups and subscriptions. As with NSGs, lower numbers take precedence.

questions.stem: What makes an Azure Virtual WAN hub a secured virtual hub?
options: Deploying an Azure Firewall, supported NVA, or SaaS security solution in the hub
Enabling DDoS Network Protection on the hub
Attaching an NSG to the hub's GatewaySubnet
Upgrading the virtual WAN from Standard to Premium
questions.explain: A secured hub has Azure Firewall, a supported NGFW NVA, or a SaaS firewall in it, typically with security and routing policies from Firewall Manager. DDoS and NSGs don't make it a secured hub, and Virtual WAN types are Basic and Standard, not Premium.

questions.stem: You have Azure Firewall in two Virtual WAN hubs. Traffic between VNets connected to different hubs must be inspected by the firewalls. What should you configure?
options: UDRs on every spoke VNet pointing to the local hub firewall
VNet peering between the spoke VNets
A private traffic routing policy (routing intent) on both hubs
An internet traffic routing policy on one hub only
questions.explain: Routing intent with a private traffic policy sends VNet, branch and inter-hub traffic through the firewall; it must be enabled on all hubs for symmetric inter-hub inspection. UDRs in spokes aren't how Virtual WAN routes, peering bypasses the hubs, and an internet policy doesn't cover private traffic.

questions.stem: For each statement about Virtual WAN security, select Yes if true.

statements.s: A Basic virtual WAN supports deploying Azure Firewall in its hub.
A hub can have at most one internet traffic routing policy and one private traffic routing policy.
Azure Firewall Manager can be used to convert a Virtual WAN hub into a secured virtual hub.

questions.explain: Basic Virtual WAN supports only site-to-site VPN; Azure Firewall needs Standard. Each hub has at most one of each routing policy, each with a single next hop. Firewall Manager converts hubs to secured hubs and associates firewall policies.

questions.stem: Your security baseline requires that a site-to-site VPN connection use AES256, SHA384 and DH group 24. The gateway SKU is VpnGw2AZ. What should you configure?
options: A custom IPsec/IKE policy on the connection
Point-to-site OpenVPN with certificate authentication
Forced tunneling on the gateway
An Azure Firewall Premium IDPS policy
questions.explain: A custom IPsec/IKE policy on the connection specifies the exact IKE and IPsec algorithms and DH/PFS groups. P2S settings don't affect S2S tunnels, forced tunneling controls internet routing, and IDPS inspects traffic rather than tunnel cryptography.

questions.stem: Which two statements about custom IPsec/IKE policies on Azure VPN Gateway are true? Select TWO.
options: Each connection can have only one policy combination
Custom policies are supported on the Basic SKU
You can set only the IKE parameters and let Azure pick the IPsec parameters
The policy applies to every connection on the gateway automatically
All IKE and IPsec parameters must be specified
questions.explain: A custom policy is set per connection, one per connection, and partial policies aren't allowed, so every parameter must be given. The Basic SKU doesn't support custom policies, and each connection is configured separately.

questions.stem: Complete the PowerShell that builds a custom IPsec/IKE policy before applying it to a connection.
questions.code:
$policy = ____ -IkeEncryption AES256 -IkeIntegrity SHA384 `
  -DhGroup DHGroup24 -IpsecEncryption GCMAES256 `
  -IpsecIntegrity GCMAES256 -PfsGroup PFS24 `
  -SALifeTimeSeconds 27000 -SADataSizeKilobytes 102400000
options: New-AzVpnClientIpsecParameter
New-AzIpsecPolicy
New-AzFirewallPolicy
New-AzVirtualNetworkGatewayConnection
questions.explain: New-AzIpsecPolicy creates the policy object, which you assign to the connection's IpsecPolicies and save with Set-AzVirtualNetworkGatewayConnection. New-AzVpnClientIpsecParameter is for P2S client parameters, New-AzFirewallPolicy is Azure Firewall, and New-AzVirtualNetworkGatewayConnection creates a connection rather than a policy object.

questions.stem: You want point-to-site VPN users to authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID. Which tunnel type must the gateway use?
options: IKEv2
SSTP
OpenVPN
L2TP
questions.explain: Microsoft Entra ID authentication for P2S works only with the OpenVPN tunnel type and the Azure VPN Client. IKEv2 and SSTP support certificate and RADIUS authentication, and L2TP isn't an Azure P2S tunnel type.

questions.case: Litware's remote staff connect to Azure with point-to-site VPN using certificate authentication. After a laptop theft, the CISO requires MFA and a compliant device for every VPN connection, managed with the same policies used for Microsoft 365.
questions.stem: What should you do?
options: Add the stolen laptop's certificate thumbprint to the revocation list and keep certificate authentication
Switch the gateway to Microsoft Entra ID authentication with OpenVPN and apply a Conditional Access policy to the Azure VPN app
Switch the gateway to IKEv2 with RADIUS authentication
Enable a custom IPsec/IKE policy with stronger algorithms
questions.explain: Entra ID P2S authentication lets Conditional Access require MFA and compliant devices, matching Microsoft 365 policies. Revoking one certificate helps but doesn't add MFA or device checks. RADIUS doesn't use Conditional Access, and IPsec policy strength doesn't verify users or devices.

questions.stem: For each statement about point-to-site VPN, select Yes if true.

statements.s: The Basic VPN gateway SKU supports RADIUS authentication.
A gateway can have several authentication types enabled at the same time.
OpenVPN can traverse most firewalls because it uses TCP 443.

questions.explain: Basic doesn't support RADIUS, IKEv2 or OpenVPN P2S. Multiple authentication types can be enabled, with each client using a compatible type. OpenVPN runs over TLS on TCP 443, so it passes most firewalls.

questions.stem: Which component of Microsoft Entra Private Access is installed on a Windows server in the private network and makes only outbound connections to the service?
options: Global Secure Access client
Azure VPN Client
Private network connector
Azure Arc Connected Machine agent
questions.explain: The private network connector runs on Windows Server near the apps and connects outbound on 443, so no inbound ports are opened. The Global Secure Access client runs on user devices. The Azure VPN Client is for P2S VPN, and the Arc agent manages servers.

questions.stem: You are replacing a VPN with Microsoft Entra Private Access. Initially, all users should reach the whole 10.0.0.0/8 range through one app. Which app type should you create?
options: Quick Access
A per-app access enterprise application for each server
An Application Proxy web app
A Conditional Access named location
questions.explain: Quick Access holds the broad set of FQDNs and IP ranges you always want tunnelled, which suits initial VPN replacement. Per-app access is for granular segments with different policies. Application Proxy publishes web apps, and named locations aren't apps.

questions.case: Tailspin uses Quick Access for 10.0.0.0/8. The finance SQL server at 10.5.1.20 must now require a compliant device and phishing-resistant MFA, while other internal resources keep their current policies.
questions.stem: What should you do?
options: Add a Conditional Access policy to the Quick Access app requiring a compliant device
Create an NSG rule that allows only compliant devices to 10.5.1.20
Install a second private network connector next to the SQL server
Create a per-app access application for 10.5.1.20:1433 with its own assignments and Conditional Access policy
questions.explain: A per-app access app segment overlapping Quick Access takes priority, so its own Conditional Access applies only to the finance server. A policy on Quick Access would affect everything. NSGs can't evaluate device compliance, and adding a connector doesn't change policy.

questions.stem: You are configuring Microsoft Entra Private Access for the first time. Put the steps in order.
options: Install a private network connector and add it to a connector group
Create the Quick Access app with application segments and select the connector group
Assign users and groups to the app
Create Conditional Access policies for the app
Enable the Private Access traffic forwarding profile
questions.explain: Apps need an active connector group before they can be created. Segments define what is tunnelled, then users are assigned and protected with Conditional Access. Enabling the forwarding profile last starts sending client traffic once everything is in place.

questions.stem: Which two Microsoft Entra roles are required to configure Quick Access for Microsoft Entra Private Access? Select TWO.
options: Hybrid Identity Administrator
Security Operator
Application Administrator
Global Secure Access Administrator
Conditional Access Administrator
questions.explain: Configuring Quick Access needs Global Secure Access Administrator and Application Administrator; Application Administrator also manages connector groups. Conditional Access Administrator manages policies but not Private Access apps, and the other roles are unrelated.

questions.stem: Which feature gives an Azure SQL logical server a private IP address inside your virtual network?
options: A virtual network service endpoint
A server-level IP firewall rule
A service endpoint policy
A private endpoint
questions.explain: A private endpoint places a NIC with a private IP in your subnet mapped to the server through Private Link. Service endpoints keep the public IP while identifying your subnet, IP rules filter public access, and service endpoint policies restrict storage destinations.

questions.stem: A storage account with hierarchical namespace has a private endpoint for the blob sub-resource. Applications that use the Data Lake Storage (dfs) endpoint still go over the public endpoint. What should you do?
options: Add the dfs endpoint to the existing private endpoint's DNS zone
Create another private endpoint with the dfs target sub-resource
Enable the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint on the subnet
Set the existing private endpoint's network policy to Enabled
questions.explain: Each storage sub-resource (blob, dfs, file, queue, table, web) needs its own private endpoint and zone. Adding records to the blob zone is wrong, a service endpoint doesn't give a private IP, and network policies control NSG/UDR enforcement, not sub-resources.

questions.stem: You need NSG rules to apply to private endpoints in subnet snet-pe. Complete the Azure CLI command.
questions.code:
az network vnet subnet update \
  --resource-group rg-net --vnet-name vnet-hub \
  --name snet-pe \
  ____
options: --private-endpoint-network-policies NetworkSecurityGroupEnabled
--private-link-service-network-policies Enabled
--service-endpoints Microsoft.Network
--disable-private-endpoint-network-policies true
questions.explain: Setting private endpoint network policies to NetworkSecurityGroupEnabled makes NSG rules apply to private endpoints (Enabled would apply NSGs and UDRs). The Private Link service setting is for publishing services, Microsoft.Network isn't a service endpoint, and disabling policies is the default that ignores NSGs.

questions.case: An on-premises application connects over ExpressRoute private peering to an Azure Key Vault. Security requires that the vault be unreachable from the internet and that only that specific vault, not others, be reachable over the private path.
questions.stem: Which two actions should you take? Select TWO.
options: Enable the Microsoft.KeyVault service endpoint on the GatewaySubnet
Create a private endpoint for the vault with the vault sub-resource
Assign the Key Vault Secrets User role to the on-premises network
Add the on-premises public IP range to the key vault firewall
Disable public network access on the key vault
questions.explain: A private endpoint gives private, resource-specific access that works over ExpressRoute, and disabling public network access removes internet reachability. Service endpoints don't extend to on-premises traffic. IP rules keep the public endpoint open, and RBAC roles are assigned to identities, not networks.

questions.stem: Which private DNS zone should be linked to a VNet so that clients resolve an Azure SQL Database private endpoint?
options: privatelink.sql.azure.com
privatelink.database.windows.net
privatelink.blob.core.windows.net
privatelink.vaultcore.azure.net
questions.explain: Azure SQL Database (sqlServer sub-resource) uses privatelink.database.windows.net. privatelink.blob.core.windows.net is for blob storage and privatelink.vaultcore.azure.net for Key Vault. privatelink.sql.azure.com isn't the recommended zone for SQL Database.

questions.stem: After you create a blob private endpoint and disable public network access, a VM in a peered spoke VNet gets 403 errors because contoso.blob.core.windows.net resolves to a public IP. VMs in the hub VNet work. What should you do?
options: Change the app's connection string to contoso.privatelink.blob.core.windows.net
Add the spoke subnet as a virtual network rule on the storage account
Link the privatelink.blob.core.windows.net private DNS zone to the spoke VNet
Create a second private endpoint in the spoke VNet
questions.explain: The spoke VNet isn't linked to the private DNS zone, so it follows the public CNAME chain. Linking the zone (or centralizing DNS) fixes resolution. Changing connection strings isn't recommended, VNet rules apply to the public endpoint that is disabled, and a second endpoint is unnecessary across peering.

questions.stem: For each statement about private endpoint DNS, select Yes if true.

statements.s: Applications should keep using the service's normal FQDN, such as contoso.blob.core.windows.net.
Successfully resolving the privatelink CNAME from the internet grants access to the resource.
A private DNS zone group on the private endpoint can create its A record in the private zone automatically.

questions.explain: Connection strings stay unchanged; DNS steers them to the private IP. The public CNAME chain is resolvable anywhere but grants nothing, since public access rules still block callers. A DNS zone group manages the A record automatically.

questions.case: Adatum's on-premises servers use on-premises DNS servers and reach Azure over ExpressRoute. A storage account has a blob private endpoint in the hub VNet, with privatelink.blob.core.windows.net linked to the hub. On-premises servers still resolve the storage account to its public IP.
questions.stem: What should you implement?
options: An Azure DNS Private Resolver inbound endpoint in the hub, with on-premises DNS conditionally forwarding blob.core.windows.net to it
A hosts file entry on one domain controller pointing at the public IP
A public DNS A record for contoso.blob.core.windows.net pointing to the private IP
A service endpoint for Microsoft.Storage on the GatewaySubnet
questions.explain: On-premises DNS must forward the storage zone to a resolver inside Azure that can see the linked private zone; Private Resolver's inbound endpoint provides that. A public IP hosts entry is wrong, you can't create records in Microsoft's public zones, and service endpoints don't serve on-premises clients.

questions.stem: What must sit in front of an application before you can publish it with Azure Private Link service?
options: An Azure Application Gateway
A Basic Load Balancer
A Standard Load Balancer
An Azure Firewall
questions.explain: Private Link service attaches to the frontend IP configuration of a Standard Load Balancer. Basic Load Balancer isn't supported. Application Gateway has its own Private Link feature, and Azure Firewall isn't a Private Link service frontend.

questions.stem: You publish a service with Azure Private Link service. Customers' subscriptions are in other Microsoft Entra tenants and have no permissions on your resources. Requests from two named customer subscriptions should be approved automatically, and other customers shouldn't be able to find the service. How should you configure it?
options: Set visibility to Anyone with your alias and leave auto-approval empty
Set visibility to Role-based access control only and add the subscriptions to auto-approval
Set visibility to Restricted by subscription and add both subscriptions to the visibility and auto-approval lists
Disable the privateLinkServiceNetworkPolicies setting and share the alias publicly
questions.explain: Restricted by subscription limits who can see and request the service, and the auto-approval list approves those subscriptions automatically. Anyone with your alias is public. RBAC only is for consumers who already hold RBAC permissions, typically in your own tenant. The subnet setting doesn't control visibility.

questions.stem: An application published through Private Link service logs only NAT IP addresses as the client source. The security team needs the consumer's original source IP. What should you enable?
options: TCP Proxy v2 on the Private Link service, and parse the PROXY header in the app
Floating IP on the load balancer rule
Private endpoint network policies on the consumer subnet
More NAT IP addresses on the Private Link service
questions.explain: TCP Proxy v2 adds a PROXY protocol header carrying the consumer source IP and LinkID; the app must parse it. Floating IP and consumer subnet policies don't preserve source IP through Private Link, and more NAT IPs just add port capacity.

questions.stem: For each statement about Azure Private Link service, select Yes if true.

statements.s: Consumers can connect even if their VNet address space overlaps the provider's VNet.
When deploying with Azure CLI, privateLinkServiceNetworkPolicies must be Disabled on the subnet hosting the service.
A consumer's private endpoint passes traffic while its connection is still in the Pending state.

questions.explain: Private Link NATs consumer traffic, so overlapping address spaces aren't a problem. The portal disables the subnet policy automatically, but CLI, PowerShell and templates need it set. Only approved connections pass traffic.

questions.case: Woodgrove hosts a payments API on VMs in its own VNet. Ten bank customers, each in their own Microsoft Entra tenant, must reach the API privately from their VNets. Several customers use 10.0.0.0/16, the same range as Woodgrove's VNet. Woodgrove must approve each customer.
questions.stem: What should you use?
options: Global VNet peering with each customer VNet
A site-to-site VPN connection to each customer
Azure Private Link service behind a Standard Load Balancer, with customers creating private endpoints
Service endpoints with VNet rules for each customer subnet
questions.explain: Private Link service supports cross-tenant consumers, overlapping address spaces and per-connection approval. Peering and VPNs fail with overlapping ranges and expose more of the network. Service endpoints apply to Azure PaaS services, not a customer-hosted API.

questions.stem: In what order does Azure Firewall process rule collections in a firewall policy?
options: Application rules, network rules, then DNAT rules
Network rules, DNAT rules, then application rules
Strictly by rule collection priority, regardless of type
DNAT rules, network rules, then application rules
questions.explain: Azure Firewall makes passes in the order DNAT, network, then application, with priorities applied within each type. Priority alone doesn't decide across types, so a low-priority network rule still runs before any application rule.

questions.stem: A child firewall policy has a rule collection group at priority 100 that allows a site. Its parent policy has a rule collection group at priority 500 that denies the same site with the same rule type. What happens?
options: The site is allowed because 100 is the higher priority
The site is denied because parent policy rule collection groups always take precedence
The site is allowed because child policies override the parent
Deployment fails because the policies conflict
questions.explain: Rule collection groups from the parent policy are always processed before those in the child, whatever the priority numbers, so the parent's Deny matches first. Child policies inherit but can't override parent rules, and the conflict doesn't block deployment.

questions.stem: Which two Azure Firewall features require at least the Standard SKU and aren't available in Basic? Select TWO.
options: DNS proxy
Web categories
Application-level FQDN filtering for HTTPS
FQDN tags
Service tags in network rules
questions.explain: DNS proxy and web categories need Standard or Premium. Basic supports application FQDN filtering, FQDN tags and service tags. Basic's threat intelligence can only alert, not deny.

questions.stem: You will route all outbound internet traffic from spoke VNets through Azure Firewall in a hub VNet. Put the steps in order.
options: Create a subnet named AzureFirewallSubnet (/26) in the hub VNet
Deploy Azure Firewall with a firewall policy into that subnet
Add application and network rule collections that allow approved traffic
Create a route table with 0.0.0.0/0 to the firewall's private IP and associate it with spoke subnets
questions.explain: The firewall needs its dedicated /26 subnet first, then the firewall and policy. Allow rules should exist before traffic is redirected, or legitimate traffic is denied by default. Finally, UDRs in spokes send traffic to the firewall's private IP.

questions.stem: Azure Firewall uses resource-specific logs in Log Analytics. Complete the KQL query to find denied network rule traffic to port 3389.
questions.code:
____
| where Action == "Deny" and DestinationPort == 3389
| summarize count() by SourceIp, Rule
options: AZFWApplicationRule
AZFWNetworkRule
AZFWThreatIntel
AzureActivity
questions.explain: AZFWNetworkRule records network rule matches with Action, SourceIp, DestinationPort and Rule. AZFWApplicationRule covers FQDN-based application rules, AZFWThreatIntel records threat intelligence hits, and AzureActivity is the control plane log.

questions.stem: You must publish an internal server's RDP port through the Azure Firewall public IP for a vendor's fixed IP address. Which rule type should you create?
options: An application rule
A network rule
A DNAT rule
A threat intelligence allowlist entry
questions.explain: DNAT rules translate inbound traffic on the firewall's public IP and port to a private IP and port, and can restrict the source. Application rules don't apply to inbound connections, network rules filter but don't translate, and the allowlist only exempts traffic from threat intelligence.

questions.stem: You are enabling TLS inspection on Azure Firewall Premium. How should the firewall access the intermediate CA certificate stored in Azure Key Vault?
options: A system-assigned managed identity with the Key Vault Certificates Officer role
A user-assigned managed identity with Get and List permissions on secrets
A service principal with a client secret stored in the firewall policy
The firewall's public IP added to the key vault firewall
questions.explain: Azure Firewall reads the CA through the Secrets interface using a user-assigned managed identity with secret Get and List. Certificate permissions alone aren't enough, a system identity isn't the documented option, and network access doesn't grant authorization.

questions.stem: Which two features require Azure Firewall Premium? Select TWO.
options: Full URL path filtering on HTTPS traffic
Threat intelligence in Alert and deny mode
IDPS that can alert on and deny malicious traffic
DNS proxy
Network rules with FQDNs
questions.explain: IDPS and full-path URL filtering (which needs TLS inspection) are Premium-only. Threat intelligence deny mode, DNS proxy and network-level FQDN filtering are available in Standard.

questions.stem: What is the default threat intelligence mode on Azure Firewall Standard and Premium?
options: Off
Alert and deny
Deny only
Alert only
questions.explain: Threat intelligence defaults to Alert only, logging matches with known malicious IPs and domains without blocking. You can switch to Alert and deny or turn it off. Deny only isn't a mode.

questions.stem: For each statement about Azure Firewall Premium, select Yes if true.

statements.s: Azure Firewall Premium performs TLS inspection on inbound internet traffic to web apps.
Threat intelligence filtering is evaluated before NAT, network and application rules.
Without TLS inspection, IDPS can't see signatures inside encrypted HTTPS payloads.

questions.explain: Premium inspects outbound and east-west TLS; inbound TLS inspection is done by Application Gateway WAF. Threat intelligence runs before configured rules. IDPS can only match payload signatures in traffic it can read, so encrypted payloads need TLS inspection.

questions.stem: Which Network Watcher tool tells you whether a specific TCP flow to a VM is allowed or denied and names the security rule responsible?
options: Next hop
IP flow verify
Connection monitor
Traffic analytics
questions.explain: IP flow verify tests a 5-tuple against the NSGs and admin rules on the VM's NIC and returns allowed or denied with the rule name. Next hop checks routing, Connection monitor tracks reachability over time, and Traffic analytics visualizes flow logs.

questions.case: Users report that a VM can't reach an internet API. IP flow verify shows outbound TCP 443 is allowed. The spokes are supposed to send internet traffic through an NVA, and a recent change added route tables.
questions.stem: Which Network Watcher tool should you use next?
options: Effective security rules
NSG diagnostics
Next hop
VPN troubleshoot
questions.explain: Security rules allow the flow, so routing is the next suspect; Next hop shows the next hop type and route table used. Effective security rules and NSG diagnostics would only repeat the security check, and VPN troubleshoot is for gateways.

questions.stem: Which three sources of rules are included in a network interface's effective security rules in Network Watcher? Select THREE.
options: The NSG associated with the subnet
The NSG associated with the network interface
Azure Firewall network rules
Route table user-defined routes
Azure Virtual Network Manager security admin rules applied to the VNet
questions.explain: Effective security rules aggregate the NIC NSG, the subnet NSG and AVNM admin rules on the VNet. Azure Firewall rules are evaluated by the firewall, not the NIC, and UDRs are routes, shown by effective routes or Next hop.

questions.stem: Complete the Azure CLI command to test whether inbound TCP 22 from 203.0.113.10 to VM vm-web is allowed.
questions.code:
az network watcher ____ \
  --resource-group rg-web --vm vm-web \
  --direction Inbound --protocol TCP \
  --local 10.0.1.4:22 --remote 203.0.113.10:50000
options: show-next-hop
test-connectivity
show-topology
test-ip-flow
questions.explain: az network watcher test-ip-flow runs IP flow verify with direction, protocol, and local and remote IP:port. show-next-hop checks routing, test-connectivity runs connection troubleshoot from the VM outward, and show-topology lists resources.

questions.stem: Before deploying Microsoft 365 Copilot, you need a report of SharePoint items and groups shared with Everyone except external users over the last 28 days. What should you use?
options: SharePoint Advanced Management data access governance reports
Microsoft Entra access reviews
Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps file policies
Microsoft Purview Content explorer
questions.explain: DAG reports in SharePoint Advanced Management include EEEU insights and sharing-link activity for the last 28 days. Entra access reviews recertify group or app membership, not SharePoint sharing. Content explorer shows where classified content lives, not EEEU exposure. Defender for Cloud Apps file policies are a different, CASB-based tool.

questions.stem: For each statement about Copilot and SharePoint oversharing, select Yes if true.

statements.s: Microsoft 365 Copilot can return content to a user only if that user already has permission to access it.
A sharing links DAG report shows which sites had the most new sharing links created recently.
Assigning a Copilot license automatically removes Everyone except external users permissions from sites.

questions.explain: Copilot respects existing permissions, which is why oversharing matters. The sharing links report shows link-creation hotspots. Licensing Copilot changes no permissions; admins must fix exposure themselves.

questions.stem: A finance site is overshared. Copilot launches tomorrow, and the permission cleanup will take weeks. Users who legitimately work on the site must keep opening its files. What should you configure right away?
options: Restricted access control for the site
A retention policy on the site
Restricted Content Discovery for the site
Delete the site's sharing links
questions.explain: Restricted Content Discovery keeps the site's content out of Copilot and organization-wide search, while people with access can still open the files. Restricted access control would limit who can open the site. Retention policies don't affect discovery. Deleting every link breaks legitimate access and doesn't scale overnight.

questions.stem: You want the owners of overshared SharePoint sites, who know their business audiences, to confirm or remove permissions found in a DAG report. Which feature should you use?
options: Restricted SharePoint Search
Site access review
Microsoft Entra entitlement management
Microsoft Purview Insider Risk Management
questions.explain: Site access review is launched from a DAG report and sends the permission review to the site owners. Restricted SharePoint Search limits which sites org-wide search and Copilot can use, but nobody reviews anything. Entitlement management handles access packages. Insider Risk Management detects risky user behaviour.

questions.case: Contoso is piloting Microsoft 365 Copilot. An M&A site must be openable only by members of the Deal-Team group, even though some files inside it were shared with 'people in your organization' links. A separate archive site is broadly accessible but should simply never appear in Copilot answers.
questions.stem: Which TWO controls meet the requirements? Select TWO.
options: Restricted access control on the M&A site
Restricted Content Discovery on the archive site
Restricted Content Discovery on the M&A site
A sensitivity label with no encryption on the archive site
Site access review on the archive site
questions.explain: Restricted access control limits the M&A site to the Deal-Team group, whatever links exist on items inside. Restricted Content Discovery keeps the archive out of Copilot and search without changing who can access it. RCD on the M&A site wouldn't stop members of the org opening links. A label without encryption or DLP doesn't stop Copilot, and a site access review doesn't hide the archive.

questions.stem: In Microsoft Purview DSPM for AI, which feature activates a recommended, preconfigured DLP policy for AI interactions with one selection?
options: Data risk assessment
Activity explorer
Adaptive scopes
One-click policies
questions.explain: One-click policies turn on recommended preconfigured policies, such as DLP for sensitive data in AI prompts, directly from DSPM. Data risk assessments find oversharing. Activity explorer shows events. Adaptive scopes define dynamic policy targets in retention and other solutions.

questions.stem: DSPM for AI shows Microsoft 365 Copilot interactions but no activity for users pasting data into third-party generative AI websites. Which TWO prerequisites should you complete? Select TWO.
options: Onboard devices to Microsoft Purview
Enable Defender for AI Services on the subscription
Install the Microsoft Purview browser extension
Assign users a Microsoft 365 Copilot license
Create a Microsoft Foundry project
questions.explain: Activity on third-party AI sites needs devices onboarded to Purview (endpoint DLP) and the Purview browser extension. Copilot licenses only cover Copilot activity. Defender for AI Services and Foundry projects protect Azure-hosted AI workloads, not users browsing to consumer AI sites.

questions.stem: For each statement about DSPM for AI data risk assessments, select Yes if true.

statements.s: A default data risk assessment runs weekly against the top 100 SharePoint sites by usage.
Custom data risk assessments refresh automatically every day indefinitely.
Restricted Content Discovery is one of the remediation options offered for overshared sites.

questions.explain: The default assessment runs weekly on the top 100 sites without being activated. Custom assessments return results once (after about 48 hours), don't refresh, and expire after 30 days, so you duplicate them to run again. Remediation options include SharePoint Restricted Content Discovery, labels and removing sharing links.

questions.stem: Copilot Studio real-time protection is configured with Microsoft Defender. At what moment does Defender evaluate the agent's activity?
options: After the response is shown to the user
Before each planned tool invocation runs
Only when the agent is published
During the nightly batch audit of conversation transcripts
questions.explain: The agent sends its planned tool call (inputs and metadata) to the threat-detection endpoint before running it, and Defender returns allow or block. Evaluating after the response or overnight would be too late to stop the action. Publishing isn't a runtime check.

questions.stem: You are enabling real-time protection for Copilot Studio agents with Microsoft Defender. Put the steps in order.
options: In the Defender portal, turn on Security for AI agents and real-time protection, then copy the Defender URL
In the Power Platform admin center, enable Microsoft Defender - Copilot Studio AI Agents with that URL and an Entra app
Give the generated App ID to the security engineer
Enter the App ID in the Defender portal and save
Confirm the status shows Connected
questions.explain: The security engineer starts in Defender and gets the URL. The Power Platform admin then sets up the trusted connection and creates the App ID. The App ID goes back into Defender, and the status should change to Connected.

questions.stem: During a Defender outage, the threat-detection endpoint for Copilot Studio agents stops responding. What happens when an agent plans a tool call?
options: The tool call is blocked and the user sees a security message
The agent pauses the conversation until the endpoint responds
The agent switches to its Foundry guardrail instead
After about one second the agent treats the call as allowed and runs the tool
questions.explain: The agent waits under 1,000 ms for a reply and then fails open, treating the call as allowed. It doesn't fail closed, it doesn't wait indefinitely, and there's no automatic fallback to a Foundry guardrail. This is why the monitor's availability matters.

questions.stem: You want to see the configuration of discovered AI agents in Advanced hunting, with only the latest record for each agent. Complete the query.
questions.code:
AIAgentsInfo
| summarize ____(Timestamp, *) by AIAgentId
| project AIAgentName, Platform, CreatorAccountUpn, IsBlocked
options: arg_max
max
make_set
dcount
questions.explain: arg_max(Timestamp, *) returns the full row with the latest Timestamp for each AIAgentId. max(Timestamp, *) isn't valid syntax for keeping all columns. make_set builds arrays. dcount counts distinct values.

questions.stem: You create a Conditional Access policy that targets agent identities which authenticate as themselves (app-only). Which grant control can you configure?
options: Require multifactor authentication
Require device to be marked as compliant
Block access
Require authentication strength
questions.explain: Block access is the only grant control for agent identities, because an agent can't complete interactive remediation such as MFA. Device compliance applies to agent user accounts, not agent identities. MFA and authentication strengths need an interactive user.

questions.stem: For each statement about Conditional Access for Microsoft Entra Agent ID, select Yes if true.

statements.s: A policy that targets an agent identity blueprint also applies to agent identities created from it in the future.
A policy assigned to All users automatically includes agent user accounts.
Agent risk is the condition you can use when a policy targets agent identities.

questions.explain: Blueprint targeting covers current and future agents created from the blueprint. Policies scoped to All users don't apply to agent users, so you target agents explicitly. Agent risk (with ID Protection) is the only condition for agent identities.

questions.case: Fabrikam allows only agents built from its approved 'Finance-Bot' blueprint to reach finance resources. Developers keep creating new agent identities from other blueprints, and security wants any agent with high agent risk blocked from everything. Agents call APIs app-only.
questions.stem: Which approach meets the requirements with the least ongoing administration?
options: Create a block policy for each new agent identity as developers register it
Target All users and exclude the Finance-Bot service principals
Require a compliant device for all agent identities accessing finance apps
Block all agent identities from finance resources except the Finance-Bot blueprint, and block high agent risk for all agent resources
questions.explain: Targeting by blueprint and using an exclusion covers future agents automatically, and an agent-risk policy blocks high-risk agents everywhere. Writing a policy per agent doesn't scale. All users doesn't target agent identities. Device compliance doesn't apply to app-only agent identities.

questions.stem: An agent reads an internal service using a static API key instead of a Microsoft Entra token. A Conditional Access policy blocks the agent identity, but the calls still succeed. Why?
options: Conditional Access needs Continuous Access Evaluation enabled for agents
Conditional Access is evaluated only when Entra ID issues tokens, and API keys bypass token issuance
The policy must be in report-only mode first
Agent identities can only be blocked by ID Protection risk policies
questions.explain: Conditional Access runs when Microsoft Entra ID issues or refreshes a token. A resource reached with an API key never involves Entra, so CA can't apply. CAE speeds up enforcement for tokens but doesn't cover key-based access. Report-only mode doesn't enforce anything.

questions.stem: You are assessing the blast radius of a Microsoft Foundry agent in Defender XDR. Which THREE factors make up the agent's blast radius? Select THREE.
options: API permissions on the agent's service principal
Knowledge sources the agent uses for grounding
The model's token-per-minute quota
Actions defined in the agent's blueprint, such as sending email
The region where the Foundry resource is deployed
questions.explain: Blast radius combines permissions (scopes), knowledge sources (the data it can reach) and blueprint actions (what it can do). TPM quotas limit cost and throughput, not what an attacker could reach. The deployment region doesn't change reach.

questions.stem: You need to review the permission breadth and knowledge sources of Copilot Studio agents in Microsoft Defender XDR. Where should you look?
options: The prebuilt AI Agents queries in Advanced hunting
The agent detail pane's View on map attack path
Microsoft Secure Score improvement actions
Defender for Cloud regulatory compliance
questions.explain: For Copilot Studio agents, the AI Agents inventory supports discovery only. You review posture with the prebuilt AI Agents queries in Advanced hunting, using tables such as AIAgentsInfo. The detail pane and attack-path map are for Foundry, Bedrock and Vertex agents. Secure Score and regulatory compliance don't show per-agent blast radius.

questions.stem: Defender XDR shows two attack paths from compromised agents: a seven-step path ending at internal meeting notes, and a three-step path ending at a database of customer financial records. Which should you remediate first, and why?
options: The seven-step path, because longer paths include more vulnerable assets
Both equally, because attack paths are scored only by count
The three-step path, because paths are prioritized by target criticality
Neither, until Secure Score drops below the threshold
questions.explain: Attack paths are ranked by how critical the target is, not by how complex the path is. A short path to customer financial data is the bigger risk. The number of steps doesn't make a path more urgent, and waiting for a Secure Score change isn't a valid prioritization method.

questions.stem: Which relationship must be assigned when an agent identity is created in Microsoft Entra Agent ID?
options: Owner
Manager
Sponsor
Application administrator
questions.explain: A sponsor is required for agent identities and agent identity blueprints. It's the human accountable for the agent's business purpose. Owners and managers are optional. Application administrator is an RBAC role, not a per-agent relationship.

questions.stem: A sponsor accidentally soft-deletes an agent identity. Who can restore it?
options: The sponsor, from the My Account portal
An owner of the agent identity (or an administrator)
The agent's manager
Any user with a Microsoft 365 Copilot license
questions.explain: Sponsors can disable or soft-delete an agent but can't re-enable or restore it. Only owners (or admins) can restore or hard-delete. Managers can't modify or delete agents, and a Copilot license grants no rights over agent objects.

questions.stem: You configure an Entra ID Governance access package for AI agents. Which TWO statements are correct? Select TWO.
options: The agent itself can request the package programmatically through Microsoft Graph
Access packages can grant agents only security group membership
The agent's sponsor can request the package on its behalf in My Access
Agent assignments cannot have an expiration date
Agent identities must be added to a role-assignable group before requesting
questions.explain: Requests can come from the agent through Graph, from a sponsor or owner in My Access, or from an admin who assigns directly. Packages can also grant OAuth API permissions and Entra roles, not just groups. Assignments can expire after the sponsor is notified. There's no role-assignable group requirement.

questions.stem: Which Azure API Management policy enforces a tokens-per-minute limit on large language model API calls?
options: rate-limit-by-key
llm-token-limit
quota-by-key
llm-emit-token-metric
questions.explain: llm-token-limit enforces TPM or token quotas using a counter key. rate-limit-by-key and quota-by-key count calls or bandwidth, not LLM tokens. llm-emit-token-metric only reports token usage to Azure Monitor.

questions.stem: You are enabling the AI gateway for an existing Microsoft Foundry resource from the Foundry portal. Put the steps in order.
options: Go to Manage > AI Gateway and select Add AI Gateway
Select the Foundry resource and choose a new or existing v2-tier API Management instance
Name the gateway, select Add, and wait for the status to show Enabled
Add each existing project to the gateway
Set per-project token limits under Token management
questions.explain: Create the gateway against the Foundry resource and an eligible APIM instance, and wait until it's enabled. Existing projects aren't added automatically. Token limits are set per project once those projects are routed through the gateway.

questions.stem: After the AI gateway is enabled, a project's client receives HTTP 403 Forbidden from a model deployment, even though its tokens-per-minute usage is low. What is the most likely cause?
options: The project's total token quota for the period has been used up
The project has exceeded its TPM limit
The client's API Management subscription key was regenerated
Content safety blocked a prompt
questions.explain: In Foundry's AI gateway, going over the period token quota returns 403, while going over the TPM limit returns 429. A regenerated key would produce an authentication failure (401), and a content safety block isn't a quota response.

questions.stem: Where do you turn on threat protection for Microsoft Foundry generative AI workloads in Microsoft Defender for Cloud?
options: Defender for Cloud > Workload protections > Just-in-time access
Microsoft Purview portal > DSPM for AI > Policies
Defender for Cloud > Environment settings > subscription > Defender plans > AI services
Foundry portal > Guardrails > Defaults
questions.explain: Defender for AI Services is a subscription-level Defender plan that you turn on under Environment settings. JIT is for VM ports. DSPM for AI is Purview data posture. Foundry guardrails filter content but aren't the Defender threat protection plan.

questions.stem: For each statement about Defender for AI Services settings, select Yes if true.

statements.s: If Enable user prompt evidence is off, AI threat detection stops analyzing prompts.
Enable data security for AI interactions lets Microsoft Purview analyze prompts and responses, and requires a Purview license.
AI threat protection alerts can be correlated with other alerts in Microsoft Defender XDR incidents.

questions.explain: With prompt evidence off, detection still runs and only the prompt text in alerts is masked. The Purview integration is a separate setting that needs Purview licensing. Alerts flow into Defender XDR and are correlated there.

questions.case: A Foundry agent uses Azure AI Search and Bing grounding. A red team planted hidden instructions in a public web page, and the agent obeyed them after retrieving the page. The model deployment's guardrail blocks jailbreaks at user input. The agent has its own custom guardrail with only hate and violence controls.
questions.stem: What should you change to stop this attack?
options: Raise the jailbreak threshold on the model deployment's guardrail
Add an Indirect attack control at the Tool response intervention point with Annotate and block to the agent's guardrail
Add a Protected material for text control at the Output point with Annotate
Remove the agent's custom guardrail so it inherits Microsoft.DefaultV2
questions.explain: Instructions hidden in retrieved content are an indirect attack. They arrive in the tool response, and the agent's own guardrail is the only one evaluated. Changing the model's guardrail has no effect because the agent's guardrail fully overrides it. Protected material isn't injection. Removing the guardrail makes the agent inherit the model's guardrail, not DefaultV2.

questions.stem: Which TWO Foundry guardrail intervention points apply only to agents and not to model deployments? Select TWO.
options: User input
Tool call
Output
Tool response
questions.explain: Tool call and tool response (both preview) scan what an agent sends to and receives from tools, so they only apply to agents that use tools. User input and output apply to both models and agents.

questions.stem: The Data and AI security dashboard in Defender for Cloud shows no sensitive-data insights for the storage accounts that ground your Foundry apps. Which change will most likely fix this?
options: Enable Defender CSPM with the sensitive data discovery extension
Enable Defender for Servers Plan 2
Enable Microsoft Purview Audit
Assign the Security Reader role at the tenant root
questions.explain: Sensitive data insights on the dashboard come from Defender CSPM's sensitive data discovery extension. Defender for Servers covers machines. Purview Audit logs user activity but doesn't classify Azure data stores for this dashboard. Security Reader only gives read access.

questions.stem: For each statement about the Defender for Cloud Data and AI security dashboard, select Yes if true.

statements.s: It groups resources into storage assets, managed databases, hosted (IaaS) databases and AI services.
It can highlight internet-exposed resources that AI apps use for grounding.
It is located in the Microsoft 365 admin center under Agents.

questions.explain: The dashboard sorts data and AI resources into four categories and includes AI insights such as internet-exposed grounding resources. It's part of Defender for Cloud. The Microsoft 365 admin center Agents page is for agent lifecycle management.

questions.stem: A Copilot Studio agent is leaking internal pricing in Teams chats. You need to stop every user in the organization from using it immediately, while keeping the agent so you can investigate. What should you do in the Microsoft 365 admin center?
options: Permanently delete the agent
Remove the last owner of the agent
Uninstall the agent for selected users
Block the agent
questions.explain: Blocking stops the agent across the organization, including in Teams and Outlook for Copilot Studio agents, and you can undo it. Permanent deletion destroys the agent. You can't remove the last owner. Uninstalling for selected users leaves other users with access.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about managing agents in the Microsoft 365 admin center are correct? Select TWO.
options: A deleted agent can be restored within 30 days
Groups can be assigned as owners of Agent Builder agents
The AI Administrator role can approve agent requests
AI Administrators can create Conditional Access policies for agent identities
Start/Stop actions apply to every agent platform
questions.explain: Delete is a soft delete with a 30-day restore window, and AI Administrators (or Global Administrators) handle agent requests. Groups can't be owners. AI Administrators can't configure Conditional Access. Start/Stop only applies to Foundry agents.

questions.stem: Which Azure resource do you create to encrypt managed disks with a customer-managed key stored in Azure Key Vault?
options: A Key Vault access policy
A Recovery Services vault
A disk encryption set
A storage account encryption scope
questions.explain: A disk encryption set links managed disks to a customer-managed key in Key Vault or Managed HSM. An access policy is a permission model. Recovery Services vaults are for backup. Encryption scopes apply to blob storage, not managed disks.

questions.case: Northwind is building new Linux VMs for a card-payment workload. Its PCI auditor requires that every byte written by the VM, including the temp disk and host caches, is encrypted, and the architecture board prohibits any technology with an announced retirement date.
questions.stem: Which encryption option should Northwind enable on the new VMs?
options: Azure Disk Encryption with BitLocker
Server-side encryption with platform-managed keys only
Server-side encryption with a disk encryption set
Encryption at host
questions.explain: Encryption at host covers temp disks and caches and is Microsoft's recommended path for new VMs. ADE also covers them, but it retires on 15 September 2028. SSE, with either key type, doesn't encrypt temp disks or caches.

questions.stem: Before creating VMs with encryption at host, you must register the feature on the subscription. Complete the Azure CLI command.
questions.code: az feature register --namespace Microsoft.Compute --name ____
options: EncryptionAtHost
AzureDiskEncryption
TrustedLaunchByDefaultPreview
DiskEncryptionSet
questions.explain: The EncryptionAtHost feature in the Microsoft.Compute namespace has to be registered before VMs can use encryption at host. TrustedLaunchByDefaultPreview controls Trusted launch defaults for template deployments. AzureDiskEncryption and DiskEncryptionSet aren't feature flags you register.

questions.stem: You are deploying Azure Bastion Standard into an existing virtual network. What must the dedicated subnet be named?
options: GatewaySubnet
AzureBastionSubnet
BastionSubnet
AzureFirewallSubnet
questions.explain: Bastion requires a subnet named exactly AzureBastionSubnet, /26 or larger. GatewaySubnet is for VPN and ExpressRoute gateways, and AzureFirewallSubnet is for Azure Firewall. BastionSubnet isn't recognized.

questions.stem: Administrators need to connect to Azure VMs with their local SSH client through Azure Bastion, using the Azure CLI. Session recording isn't required. Which is the lowest SKU that supports this?
options: Developer
Basic
Standard
Premium
questions.explain: Native client support starts at the Standard SKU. Developer and Basic offer browser-based connections only. Premium also supports native client, but it isn't the lowest SKU that meets the need, since its extras are session recording and private-only deployment.

questions.case: Litware must give administrators RDP access to production VMs. Requirements: the VMs have no public IPs, the Bastion host itself must not have a public IP because all admins connect over ExpressRoute, and every session must be recorded for auditors.
questions.stem: Which TWO configurations meet the requirements? Select TWO.
options: Deploy Azure Bastion Premium
Use a private-only Bastion deployment
Deploy Azure Bastion Developer
Open TCP 3389 on the VM NSGs from the ExpressRoute range
Use a Standard SKU public IP on AzureBastionSubnet
questions.explain: Session recording and private-only deployment (no public IP) are both Premium-only features, so Litware needs Premium deployed as private-only. Developer has neither feature. Opening 3389 directly bypasses Bastion and its recording. A public IP contradicts the requirement.

questions.stem: Which Defender for Cloud plan must be enabled to use just-in-time VM access?
options: Defender for Servers Plan 2
Foundational CSPM
Defender for Servers Plan 1
Defender for Resource Manager
questions.explain: JIT VM access is a Defender for Servers Plan 2 feature. Plan 1 focuses on Defender for Endpoint EDR. Foundational CSPM is free posture management. Defender for Resource Manager detects suspicious ARM operations.

questions.stem: For each statement about just-in-time VM access, select Yes if true.

statements.s: By default, JIT protects ports 22, 3389, 5985 and 5986.
The default maximum request time is 24 hours.
JIT can enforce access through NSG rules, Azure Firewall rules, or both.

questions.explain: The default ports are SSH, RDP and the two WinRM ports. The default maximum request time is 3 hours, not 24. JIT works with NSGs and/or Azure Firewall, but not with firewalls managed by Firewall Manager.

questions.stem: Help desk staff must be able to request JIT access to VMs but must not be able to change JIT policies or VM configuration. Which permission must their custom role include?
options: Microsoft.Security/locations/jitNetworkAccessPolicies/write
Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachines/write
Microsoft.Security/locations/jitNetworkAccessPolicies/initiate/action
Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups/write
questions.explain: Requesting access needs the initiate/action permission, along with read permissions. The jitNetworkAccessPolicies/write and virtualMachines/write permissions configure policies. NSG write would let staff edit rules directly and bypass JIT.

questions.stem: What must be installed on an on-premises Windows server so that it can be managed with Azure Policy and protected by Defender for Cloud as an Azure Arc-enabled server?
options: Azure Connected Machine agent
Log Analytics agent
Azure VM Agent
On-premises data gateway
questions.explain: The Azure Connected Machine agent registers the server as an Arc-enabled server in Azure Resource Manager. The Log Analytics agent is retired. The Azure VM Agent runs only on Azure VMs. The on-premises data gateway connects Power Platform and Logic Apps to on-premises data.

questions.stem: You are onboarding an on-premises Windows server to Azure Arc so that Defender for Servers and Azure Policy can manage it. Put the steps in order.
questions.explain: You generate the script in Azure and run it on the server to install the Connected Machine agent. The agent registers the machine over outbound 443. Once it's an ARM resource, policy assignments and Defender for Servers apply to it like any other resource.
options: In the Azure portal, open Azure Arc > Machines > Add/Create and generate an onboarding script
Run the script on the server to install the Azure Connected Machine agent
The agent connects outbound over HTTPS and registers the server as an Arc-enabled server resource
Assign Azure Policy and Machine Configuration to the resource group, and confirm Defender for Servers coverage

questions.case: Adatum has 50 on-premises Ubuntu servers in a data centre that allows only outbound HTTPS. Security must bring them into Defender for Servers this week, and compliance requires them to be evaluated against Azure Policy guest configuration baselines just like the Azure VMs.
questions.stem: Which onboarding method should Adatum use?
options: Defender for Cloud direct onboarding with Defender for Endpoint
Install the Azure Monitor Agent only
Create a GCP connector
Azure Arc with the Connected Machine agent
questions.explain: Azure Arc makes the servers ARM resources, so both Defender for Servers and Azure Policy / Machine Configuration apply. Direct onboarding doesn't support Azure Policy or Guest Configuration. AMA alone doesn't onboard machines to Defender. A GCP connector is only for Google Cloud resources.

questions.stem: You are protecting AWS EC2 instances with Defender for Servers Plan 2, including features that need Azure Arc. Put the steps in order.
options: In Defender for Cloud Environment settings, add an AWS environment (connector)
Select the Defender for Servers plan and configure Arc auto-provisioning
Download the CloudFormation template and deploy the stack in AWS
Review and create the connector, then verify the EC2 instances appear as Arc-enabled servers
questions.explain: Create the connector in Defender for Cloud and pick the plans and settings. Deploy the generated CloudFormation stack to grant access. Then finish the connector and confirm the instances were onboarded through Arc.

questions.stem: You enable Defender for Servers Plan 2 on a subscription and need to exclude one test VM from paid coverage. What should you do?
options: Move the VM to a different region
Disable Defender for Servers on that VM resource
Remove the Defender for Endpoint extension from the VM
Switch the subscription to Plan 1
questions.explain: Plan 2 can't be enabled per resource, but you can disable it per resource. Region doesn't affect coverage. Removing the MDE extension leaves the VM billed. Switching the whole subscription to Plan 1 affects every VM.

questions.stem: Which THREE capabilities are included in Defender for Servers Plan 2 but not in Plan 1? Select THREE.
options: Defender for Endpoint EDR integration
File integrity monitoring
Agentless malware scanning
Agent-based vulnerability scanning
Just-in-time VM access
questions.explain: FIM, agentless malware scanning and JIT are Plan 2 only. Both plans include Defender for Endpoint EDR and agent-based vulnerability scanning through MDVM.

questions.stem: After you enable Defender for Servers, which built-in solution provides vulnerability assessment on machines that have the Defender for Endpoint extension, without a separate scanner?
options: Qualys vulnerability scanner (built-in)
Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management
Azure Update Manager
Microsoft Defender External Attack Surface Management
questions.explain: MDVM is turned on by default wherever the Defender for Endpoint extension is present. The built-in Qualys option has been retired. Update Manager handles patching, not vulnerability assessment. Defender EASM maps internet-facing assets, not in-guest vulnerabilities.

questions.stem: Agentless scanning returns no results for VMs whose disks are encrypted with a customer-managed key, while other VMs scan normally. What should you do?
options: Grant the Defender for Cloud Servers Scanner Resource Provider wrap and unwrap key access on the key vault
Install the Azure Monitor Agent on the VMs
Enable just-in-time access on the VMs
Assign the VM scanner operator role to the security team
questions.explain: To scan CMK-encrypted disks, the scanner resource provider needs Get, Wrap Key and Unwrap Key access, or the Key Vault Crypto Service Encryption User role. The scan is agentless, so AMA doesn't help. JIT is unrelated. The VM scanner operator role is assigned to the service automatically, not to users.

questions.stem: For each statement about agentless scanning for machines, select Yes if true.

statements.s: Agentless scanning analyzes disk snapshots and does not run code inside the VM.
Malware scanning through agentless scanning is available with Defender CSPM alone.
You can configure agentless scans to run every hour.

questions.explain: Scanning works on snapshots outside the VM. Defender CSPM includes inventory, vulnerability and secrets scanning, but agentless malware scanning needs Defender for Servers Plan 2. Scans run every 24 hours on a fixed schedule.

questions.stem: Which Trusted launch feature makes sure only signed boot loaders, kernels and kernel drivers can run on an Azure VM?
options: vTPM
Boot integrity monitoring
Encryption at host
Secure Boot
questions.explain: Secure Boot enforces signature checks on boot components. The vTPM stores keys and measures the boot chain for attestation. Boot integrity monitoring reports attestation results. Encryption at host protects disk data.

questions.stem: Complete the ARM securityProfile so the VM is deployed with Trusted launch, Secure Boot and vTPM.
options: Standard
ConfidentialVM
TrustedLaunch
SecureBoot
questions.explain: securityType TrustedLaunch together with uefiSettings turns on Secure Boot and vTPM. Standard opts out of Trusted launch. ConfidentialVM is for confidential VM sizes. SecureBoot isn't a valid securityType value.

questions.stem: Defender for Cloud must report boot integrity attestation for a VM. Which THREE are required? Select THREE.
options: Secure Boot enabled
vTPM enabled
Guest Attestation extension installed
Azure Disk Encryption enabled
A Generation 1 VM image
questions.explain: Boot integrity monitoring needs Secure Boot, vTPM and the Guest Attestation extension, all on a Gen2 Trusted launch VM. ADE isn't required. Generation 1 VMs don't support Trusted launch.

questions.stem: A Machine Configuration policy must apply a hardened setting to Windows Server VMs and automatically reverse any later manual change. Which assignment type should you use?
options: Audit
ApplyAndMonitor
DeployIfNotExists
ApplyAndAutoCorrect
questions.explain: ApplyAndAutoCorrect applies the configuration and fixes drift at each evaluation. ApplyAndMonitor applies once and only reports drift. Audit only reports. DeployIfNotExists is an Azure Policy effect, not a Machine Configuration assignment type.

questions.case: You assign a built-in Machine Configuration audit policy for the Windows security baseline to a subscription. Arc-enabled on-premises servers report compliance results within an hour, but newly deployed Azure VMs stay in a non-reporting state.
questions.stem: What is the most likely fix?
options: Install the Azure Connected Machine agent on the Azure VMs
Assign the 'Deploy prerequisites to enable Guest Configuration policies on virtual machines' initiative
Enable just-in-time VM access
Change the assignment type to ApplyAndAutoCorrect
questions.explain: Azure VMs need the machine configuration extension and a system-assigned managed identity, and the prerequisites initiative deploys both. Arc servers already have the service in their agent. The Connected Machine agent isn't for Azure VMs. JIT and a different assignment type don't fix missing prerequisites.

questions.stem: Which Defender for Containers component must be deployed to cluster nodes to detect suspicious processes running inside containers?
options: Defender sensor
Kubernetes API access
Registry access
Agentless discovery for Kubernetes
questions.explain: The Defender sensor runs on nodes and collects the runtime telemetry used for workload threat detection. Kubernetes API access and agentless discovery provide posture data. Registry access scans images for vulnerabilities.

questions.stem: You want deployments to an AKS cluster to be blocked when their container images have critical vulnerabilities found by Defender for Containers. What should you enable?
options: Defender Security Gating (gated deployment) on the Defender sensor
Image Cleaner on the cluster
API server authorized IP ranges
The ACR admin user
questions.explain: Defender Security Gating adds an admission control that uses vulnerability findings to audit or block deployments. Image Cleaner removes unused images from nodes. Authorized IP ranges limit API access. The admin user is a registry credential.

questions.stem: For each statement about onboarding clusters to Defender for Containers, select Yes if true.

statements.s: Amazon EKS clusters are onboarded through an AWS connector in Defender for Cloud.
An on-premises Kubernetes cluster must first be connected to Azure Arc.
AKS clusters must be connected to Azure Arc before Defender for Containers can protect them.

questions.explain: EKS and GKE use multicloud connectors, which create Arc-enabled Kubernetes resources. On-premises clusters need Azure Arc. AKS clusters are native Azure resources and need neither a connector nor Arc.

questions.stem: You are creating an AKS cluster where all Kubernetes access must go through Microsoft Entra ID and the static cluster-admin credentials must not exist. Complete the command.
questions.code:
az aks create --resource-group rg-prod --name aks-prod \
  --enable-aad --enable-azure-rbac \
  ____
options: --disable-local-accounts
--enable-managed-identity
--enable-private-cluster
--enable-oidc-issuer
questions.explain: --disable-local-accounts removes the local admin kubeconfig, so access has to go through Entra ID. A managed identity is the cluster's own identity. A private cluster restricts network reach, not credentials. The OIDC issuer supports workload identity.

questions.stem: Pods in an AKS cluster must call Azure Key Vault with Microsoft Entra tokens, without storing client secrets in the cluster. What should you configure?
options: Kubernetes Secrets holding a service principal secret
Microsoft Entra Workload ID with the OIDC issuer
The ACR admin user
API server authorized IP ranges
questions.explain: Workload identity federates a Kubernetes service account with an Entra identity, so pods get tokens without stored secrets. A service principal secret in a Kubernetes Secret is exactly what the requirement rules out. The ACR admin user and authorized IP ranges don't give pods an identity.

questions.case: Tailwind runs a multi-tenant AKS cluster. Requirements: the API server must not be reachable from the internet; pods in the 'payments' namespace may accept traffic only from pods in the 'frontend' namespace; and privileged containers must be rejected in the payments namespace.
questions.stem: Which THREE controls meet the requirements? Select THREE.
options: Deploy the cluster as a private cluster
Apply a Kubernetes network policy on the payments namespace
Label the payments namespace to enforce the restricted Pod Security Standard
Enable Image Cleaner
Assign the Azure Kubernetes Service RBAC Reader role to the frontend team
questions.explain: A private cluster keeps the API server off the internet. A network policy limits ingress to traffic from the frontend namespace. Pod Security Admission set to restricted rejects privileged pods. Image Cleaner removes stale images, and a reader role controls API access, not pod traffic.

questions.stem: Which Azure Container Registry service tier is required to use private endpoints?
options: Basic
Standard
Premium
Any tier, once the admin user is disabled
questions.explain: Private Link for ACR is a Premium feature. Basic and Standard registries can't use private endpoints, and the admin user setting has nothing to do with networking.

questions.stem: An AKS cluster must pull images from ACR with least privilege and no shared credentials. What should you do?
options: Enable the ACR admin user and store its password as an image pull secret
Assign AcrPush to the cluster's kubelet identity
Create a repository-scoped token with push and pull on all repositories
Assign AcrPull to the cluster's kubelet managed identity
questions.explain: AcrPull on the kubelet identity, which az aks update --attach-acr sets up, allows pulls only with no stored secret. The admin user is a shared full-access credential. AcrPush grants more than needed. A token with push rights on every repository isn't least privilege.

questions.stem: A security review finds the registry's shared admin account is enabled. Complete the command to disable it.
questions.code: az acr update --name contosoacr ____
options: --public-network-enabled false
--admin-enabled false
--anonymous-pull-enabled false
--sku Premium
questions.explain: --admin-enabled false turns off the shared admin user. --public-network-enabled false blocks public network access. --anonymous-pull-enabled false stops unauthenticated pulls. Changing the SKU doesn't affect the admin account.

questions.stem: You are deploying an Azure Container Instances container group into an existing virtual network subnet that's currently empty. What must be done to the subnet first?
options: Attach a route table that forces traffic to Azure Firewall
Enable a service endpoint for Microsoft.ContainerRegistry
Delegate the subnet to Microsoft.ContainerInstance/containerGroups
Name the subnet AzureContainerSubnet
questions.explain: VNet-deployed container groups need a subnet delegated to Microsoft.ContainerInstance/containerGroups, and only container groups can use it. There's no required subnet name. Route tables and service endpoints are optional and don't replace delegation.

questions.stem: An Azure Container Apps API must be reachable only from other apps and VMs in its virtual network, and must read its database password from Azure Key Vault without storing credentials. Which TWO configurations should you use? Select TWO.
options: Set ingress to internal
Reference the Key Vault secret using the app's managed identity
Enable the ACR admin user
Set ingress to external and allow 0.0.0.0/0
Store the password as a plain environment variable
questions.explain: Internal ingress keeps the app inside the environment's VNet. A Key Vault secret reference resolved with a managed identity avoids storing credentials. External ingress open to everyone, the ACR admin user and plain-text environment variables all break the requirements.

questions.stem: An HTTP-triggered function has authorization level 'function'. Which key can a caller use to invoke it?
options: The function's key or any host key
Only the master key
A storage account access key
No key is required
questions.explain: At the function level, either that function's key or a host key works. The master key is required only at the admin level. Storage account keys don't authorize HTTP triggers. Only the anonymous level needs no key.

questions.stem: A function app exposes HTTP APIs to employees. Security says that shared function keys don't identify who is calling, and only signed-in Microsoft Entra users should reach the code, with no code changes. What should you implement?
options: Rotate the host keys weekly
Switch the authorization level to admin
Enable App Service authentication with the Microsoft Entra identity provider
Store the function keys in Azure Key Vault
questions.explain: App Service authentication (Easy Auth) with Entra ID authenticates users before requests reach the code, with no code changes. Rotating keys or storing them in Key Vault still leaves shared secrets. The admin level just demands the master key, which is worse.

questions.stem: A Logic App action retrieves a secret from Key Vault and passes it to an HTTP action. Operators can see the secret in run history. Which configuration hides it from both actions in run history?
options: Enable Secure outputs on the Key Vault action and Secure inputs on the HTTP action
Enable Secure inputs on the Key Vault action only
Regenerate the logic app's access keys
Change the trigger to use OAuth with Microsoft Entra ID
questions.explain: Secure outputs hides the secret where it's produced, and downstream actions don't inherit that protection, so the HTTP action also needs Secure inputs. Securing only the Key Vault action's inputs leaves its output visible. Access keys and trigger OAuth control who can call the workflow, not what run history shows.

questions.stem: For each statement about securing a Consumption logic app with a Request trigger, select Yes if true.

statements.s: By default, the trigger's callback URL contains a shared access signature.
A single inbound request can authenticate with both SAS and an OAuth token at the same time.
You can restrict inbound calls so that only other logic apps can call the trigger.

questions.explain: The callback URL includes SAS parameters (sp, sv, sig) by default. SAS and OAuth can't be combined on one request, and doing so causes an error. The Allowed inbound IP addresses setting includes an 'Only other Logic Apps' option.

questions.stem: You added access restriction rules so an App Service web app accepts traffic only from your office IP range. A penetration test shows the Kudu (SCM) endpoint is still reachable from the internet. What should you do?
options: Enable HTTPS Only
Configure access restrictions for the SCM site, or set it to use the main site rules
Enable VNet integration
Turn on Defender for App Service
questions.explain: The SCM site has its own access restriction rules, so you either add rules there or tell it to use the main site's rules. HTTPS Only doesn't block anyone. VNet integration is outbound only. Defender for App Service detects threats but doesn't restrict access.

questions.stem: Complete the Azure CLI command that forces an App Service app to redirect all HTTP requests to HTTPS.
questions.code: az webapp update --resource-group rg-web --name app-contoso ____
options: --https-only true
--min-tls-version 1.2
--client-cert-enabled true
--ftps-state FtpsOnly
questions.explain: --https-only true on az webapp update turns on HTTPS-only redirection. Minimum TLS and FTPS state are set with az webapp config set. Client certificates require mTLS, which doesn't redirect HTTP.

questions.case: A web app stores a SQL connection string in app settings and is deployed with FTP using publishing profile credentials. An audit requires that no secrets are kept in app configuration and that deployments don't use shared basic credentials.
questions.stem: Which TWO actions meet the requirements? Select TWO.
options: Replace the connection string with a Key Vault reference resolved by the app's managed identity
Disable basic authentication for FTP and SCM publishing
Set the minimum TLS version to 1.3
Enable client certificate mode Required
Add an access restriction for the office IP
questions.explain: A Key Vault reference keeps the secret out of app settings, and disabling basic auth for FTP and SCM removes shared publishing credentials. TLS version, client certificates and IP restrictions are good hardening steps, but they don't meet either requirement.
